teaser: A man made of eggshell and tree trunks looks back at you from Hell. Nobody knows why.
review_notes:
Tree-Man as a possible self-portrait of Bosch: a common hypothesis, presented as unproven.
Giraffe and elephant probably copied from travelers' drawings (the giraffe is often linked to Cyriacus of Ancona): stated as 'likely'.
First record of the painting: Antonio de Beatis, 1517, palace of the Counts of Nassau in Brussels.
Early Spanish name 'painting of the strawberry / strawberry tree' (madrono), from Escorial inventory 1593 and Siguenza 1605.
Dutch proverb comparing happiness to glass, linked to the couple in the bubble: commonly cited, check wording.
Music on the sinner's backside transcribed in 2014 by Amelia Hamrick (Oklahoma Christian University); viral nickname '600-year-old butt song from hell'.
Sent to El Escorial in 1593; at the Prado since the 1930s (deposit 1939).
Dimensions open about 220 x 389 cm.
Bosch's house on the market square of 's-Hertogenbosch.
Exterior shutters read as the third day of Creation: usual reading, stated as 'probably'.
Coordinates were taken from a 1100 px wide image: the smallest spots (owl in the fountain, cat with prey, score on the backside, couple in the bubble, mussel shell) deserve a visual check in the app.

lesson.text: A man stands in the dark with his feet in two small boats. His legs are hollow tree trunks. His body is a cracked eggshell with a tavern inside, and on his head sits a disc where demons parade around a pink bagpipe. He turns his pale face over his shoulder, almost amused.
This creature hides somewhere in the painting below. Can you spot him?

spots.title: The Tree-Man
spots.text: People call him the Tree-Man. Some historians suspect the face is Bosch's own, though nothing proves it. Remember that look over the shoulder: we will come back to it.

lesson.text: Now step back. The Tree-Man is one creature among hundreds in a triptych, a painting made of three hinged panels. Open, it measures about 2.2 by 3.9 meters (roughly 7 by 13 feet). Hieronymus Bosch painted it in oil on oak around 1500.

Fold the two side panels shut and the colors vanish. The outside shows the Earth as a gray, transparent globe half filled with water, probably the world on the third day of Creation, before animals and people. Opening it was meant to be a shock.

Triptychs usually stood on church altars. This one almost certainly never did: it was first recorded in 1517 in a nobleman's palace in Brussels, a showpiece for guests. It reads like a sentence, from left to right, and Bosch built in a few clues to guide you.
Three clues to how the panels connect.

lines.label: One horizon
lines.text: The left and center panels share the same horizon, the same grass, the same sky. The crowded garden in the middle grows straight out of Eden.

lines.label: Where it breaks
lines.text: At this hinge the landscape stops. No horizon, no green, no daylight: the right panel is a night lit only by fires.

lines.label: Three centers
lines.text: Each panel has a strange structure at its heart: a pink fountain, a blue globe, the Tree-Man. A fountain of life, then a fragile toy, then a hollow shell.

lesson.text: Bosch was not his family name. He was born Jheronimus van Aken and signed with a short form of his hometown, 's-Hertogenbosch, in today's Netherlands. He spent nearly his whole life there, in a house on the market square.

So the story runs from a beginning to an end: Paradise, then a garden of pleasures, then punishment. That sounds simple. It gets less simple once you inspect Paradise itself, which ought to be the one peaceful place in the picture.

lesson.title: Trouble in Paradise
lesson.text: God has just created Eve. From a distance, everything on the left panel looks calm.

spots.title: The introduction
spots.text: God, shown young like Christ, holds Eve by the wrist and presents her to Adam, who has just woken up. Adam stares. Many viewers read that stare as the first spark of desire.

spots.title: The owl
spots.text: In the dark hole at the base of the pink fountain sits an owl. In Bosch's time an owl was a night bird of ill omen as much as a wise one. It watches from the exact middle of Eden.

spots.title: The cat
spots.text: A cat walks off with a small animal in its jaws. Nearby, creatures crawl out of a dark pond and birds squabble. Killing has already begun, before anyone has touched an apple.

spots.title: The giraffe
spots.text: Bosch never saw a giraffe or an elephant. He likely copied them from travelers' drawings, which is why this one is white and slightly off. Eden is stocked with the rarest things he knew.

lesson.text: Paradise already holds a predator and a watching owl. Bosch seems to say the trouble did not begin in the garden next door: it was planted on the first day. With that in mind, the huge center panel becomes harder to judge.

Hundreds of naked men and women ride animals, bathe, nibble giant berries and climb into shells. Nobody is old, nobody works, nobody seems ashamed. No document tells us what Bosch meant, and scholars still disagree: a warning against lust, or a dream of the world as it might be if humans had never sinned?

Whichever you choose, the evidence is in the small things, and there are far too many for a guided walk. Roam the garden on your own. Watch for fruit and birds that are bigger than people, and for anything made of glass.

spots.title: The blue globe
spots.text: At the center of the lake floats a blue globe topped with pink spires. Tiny figures climb on it and sit in its openings. It looks grand and breakable at once.

spots.title: The endless ride
spots.text: Women bathe in a round pool while men circle them on horses, boars, a camel and stranger beasts. Round and round, going nowhere: a merry-go-round of showing off.

spots.title: Lovers in a bubble
spots.text: A couple sits inside a transparent sphere that grows from a plant like a soap bubble. A Dutch saying of the time compared happiness to glass: it breaks quickly.

spots.title: Giant birds
spots.text: A kingfisher, a goldfinch and other birds tower over the bathers at the water's edge. The scale is flipped: here humans are the small animals.

spots.title: The mussel shell
spots.text: A man carries a huge mussel shell on his back, with people shut inside it. Shells, pods and hollow fruit serve as hiding places all over the garden.

spots.title: The owl again
spots.text: An owl perches above a ring of dancers. The bird that watched from the fountain in Eden has followed us into the garden.

spots.title: The giant berry
spots.text: Figures cluster around a red berry almost as big as they are. Sweet, bright, and rotten within days: a neat picture of a pleasure that does not last.

lesson.text: Everything in the garden is delicious and fragile: fruit that rots, glass that breaks, bubbles that burst. Whether Bosch disapproved or daydreamed, he painted pleasure as something that cannot last.

For centuries nobody called it The Garden of Earthly Delights. Bosch left no title. Early Spanish descriptions name the picture after its fruit, as the painting of the strawberry, and the title we use settled in much later.

How did he keep so many tiny scenes bright and readable? Bosch worked in thin, almost transparent layers of oil paint over a white ground, which makes the colors glow like enamel. Technical scans show he changed his mind as he went, redrawing figures directly on the panel.

Then comes the bill. In the right panel the lights go out, and the same species that played in the garden is hunted, eaten and mocked. Bosch's cruelest idea is that the things people enjoyed become the tools that hurt them. Start with music.

lesson.title: The night side
lesson.text: Three stops in the dark, from the top of the panel down.

spots.title: Ears and a blade
spots.text: Two giant ears carry a knife between them like a war machine rolling over the damned. What it means is anyone's guess, and that is part of its power.

spots.title: The music lesson
spots.text: Under a giant lute and harp, a sinner lies crushed, with a musical score written across his backside. The instruments of pleasure have become racks.

spots.title: The bird-headed prince
spots.text: A blue monster with a bird's head and a cauldron for a hat sits on a tall chair, swallowing a person whole. He is often called the Prince of Hell.

lesson.text: The notes on that sinner's backside are readable. In 2014 a music student in Oklahoma, Amelia Hamrick, transcribed them and posted a recording online. It spread around the world under an unofficial title: the butt song from Hell.

The painting soon became a prize. King Philip II of Spain, a devoted collector of Bosch, had it sent to his monastery-palace of El Escorial in 1593. It moved to the Prado in Madrid in the 1930s. Four centuries after Bosch, the Surrealists, painters of dreams such as Salvador Dalí, claimed him as an ancestor.

Return to the Tree-Man. Everyone else in Hell is too busy suffering to notice anything. He alone looks back, over his broken body, toward the garden and toward you. A warning, a regret, or the faint smile of a painter enjoying his own invention? Bosch never said.

quiz.question: What is a triptych?
options: A painting made of three hinged panels
A painting made in three days
quiz.explanation: The Garden is three oak panels joined by hinges, so the sides can fold shut.

quiz.question: What do the left and center panels share?
quiz.explanation: The horizon runs across both, so the garden seems to grow out of Eden.

quiz.question: What sits in the dark hole of the fountain in Eden?
quiz.explanation: An owl watches from the middle of Paradise, and another appears in the central garden.

quiz.question: What appears when the side panels are closed?
options: The Earth as a gray globe
quiz.explanation: The outside shows a colorless globe, probably the world on the third day of Creation.

quiz.question: What is written on a sinner's backside in the Hell panel?
quiz.explanation: The notes are readable, and a student transcribed and recorded them in 2014.

quiz.question: Which Spanish king sent the painting to El Escorial?
quiz.explanation: Philip II, a keen collector of Bosch, had it sent there in 1593.

facts.text: Bosch gave the painting the title The Garden of Earthly Delights.
facts.explanation: He left no title; early Spanish descriptions named it after its strawberry.

facts.text: Bosch took his name from his hometown.
facts.explanation: He was born Jheronimus van Aken and signed after 's-Hertogenbosch.

facts.text: Documents from Bosch's time explain what the central panel means.
facts.explanation: No such document exists, and scholars still disagree about it.
